title: Practice Set PRJ3 — Predicate Pushdown
description: Junior teaching track: read PushedFilters in FileScan, recognize when a UDF blocks pushdown. Companion to PS6 / PSI1 lessons on predicate pushdown.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Junior plan-reading scenarios describe NordGrid Energy at junior scale (500K meters across 4 regions, 200 substations, single cluster).
Substations reference. Used in broadcast-eligible join examples in PRJ5.

description.context: When you write a filter like .filter(col('daily_kw') > 100), you might expect Spark to load every row and then check the condition. It usually does something smarter: it tells the file reader to skip rows that fail the condition BEFORE they enter Spark's memory. This optimization is called PREDICATE PUSHDOWN. In a physical plan, look at the FileScan line for a field called PushedFilters: [...]. Filter conditions that pushed down appear in this list. Conditions that did NOT push down stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan. Pushdown matters because it can reduce data read from disk by 100× or more.
description.task: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A physical plan from a NordGrid query with two filter conditions, one pushed down and one not

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3,region#5]
      PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)]

fields.label: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?
options: Both conditions pushed down. The Filter operator above is a leftover that Spark always shows even when filters are fully pushed down to the file reader; safe to ignore.
Neither condition pushed down. PushedFilters: [...] is just a debug label; actual filtering always happens in the Filter operator above the FileScan line.
region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
daily_kw > 100 pushed down because it is in the Filter operator at the top of the plan. region == 'NORTH' did not push down because it appears below FileScan in the PushedFilters list.
fields.correctAnswer: region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)] tells you which conditions the parquet reader applied while loading.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats the residual Filter operator as inert; it is the actual second-stage filter.
Option B: Treats PushedFilters as decorative.

tasks.title: Why a UDF Filter Did Not Push Down

description.context: Not every filter can push down. For pushdown to work, Spark needs to express the condition in a form the file reader understands — equality, range comparison, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, simple boolean combinations. When you wrap a column in a Python UDF (a user-defined function), Spark cannot translate the function call into something the file reader can evaluate. The file reader is a Java/native library; it does not run Python code. So filters using UDFs always stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan, and Spark must load every row to evaluate them.
description.task: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain()

Code B: is_high = udf(lambda kw: kw > 100, 'boolean')
meters.filter(is_high(col('daily_kw'))).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two side-by-side plans from queries that look similar — one filter pushes down, one does not because of a UDF

evidence.label: Plan A — built-in comparison
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [daily_kw#3]
      PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0)]

evidence.label: Plan B — UDF wrapping the same condition
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter pythonUDF0#15: boolean
+- BatchEvalPython [is_high(daily_kw#3)#14], [pythonUDF0#15]
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [daily_kw#3]
         PushedFilters: []

fields.label: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?
options: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
Plan B's UDF correctly pushed down — BatchEvalPython is the optimized form of pushdown for Python functions. The empty PushedFilters list is misleading; Spark uses a different mechanism for UDFs.
Plan B's filter pushes down but produces wrong results because the UDF returns Python bool instead of Java Boolean; the cast in BatchEvalPython is a workaround. Cost: small CPU overhead for the cast.
Plan B is functionally identical to Plan A. BatchEvalPython is added by Catalyst even when no Python is involved; PushedFilters is empty because of an unrelated planner bug. Cost: same as Plan A.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [] in Plan B is the key signal.The parquet reader applies no filter and returns all rows.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Misreads BatchEvalPython as pushdown.It is UDF evaluation AFTER the file is read.
Option C: Invents a casting bug.
